en: Thus have I heard: the Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta, the Forty-sixth Discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, for the most part, beings have such desires, such inclinations, and such intentions as this:”
‘Oh, may unwholesome, disagreeable, and unpleasant phenomena diminish, and may wholesome, agreeable, and pleasant phenomena increase!

Yet, monks, for those beings who have such desires, such wishes, and such intentions, unwholesome, disagreeable, and unpleasant phenomena increase, while wholesome, agreeable, and pleasant phenomena diminish.
In this regard, monks, what cause do you perceive?”
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“In that case, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling, who has no regard for the noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who has no regard for true persons and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma—”

He does not know the states that should be cultivated, nor does he know the states that should not be cultivated; he does not know the states that should be frequented, nor does he know the states that should not be frequented.

Not knowing the states that should be cultivated and not knowing the states that should not be cultivated, not knowing the states that should be frequented and not knowing the states that should not be frequented, he cultivates the states that should not be cultivated and does not cultivate the states that should be cultivated.
He associates with things that should not be associated with and does not associate with things that should be associated with. For him,

by practicing what should not be practiced and not practicing what should be practiced, by associating with things that should not be associated with and not associating with things that should be associated with,
undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable states increase, while desirable and pleasing [states]...
Agreeable phenomena decline.
For what reason?
Because it is so, monks, for one who lacks true knowledge.

But the learned noble disciple, monks, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—knows the things that should be cultivated and knows the things that should not be cultivated;
knows the things that should be associated with and knows the things that should not be associated with.
Knowing the things that should be cultivated and knowing the things that should not be cultivated, knowing the things that should be associated with...
Knowing the qualities that should not be cultivated, he does not cultivate those qualities that should not be cultivated;

he cultivates those qualities that should be cultivated, and he does not associate with those qualities that should not be associated with, but associates with those qualities that should be associated with.

As he does not cultivate the qualities that should not be cultivated, as he cultivates the qualities that should be cultivated, and as he does not associate with the qualities that should not be associated with...
For one who cultivates those things that should be cultivated, things that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable decline,
while things that are desirable, lovely, and agreeable increase. Why is that?
For it is thus, monks, that it happens for one who has seen.
There are, monks, these four ways of undertaking things.
What are the four?
“Monks, there is a way of undertaking things that is painful both in the present and results in suffering in the future;
there is, monks, a way of undertaking things that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future;
there is, monks, a way of undertaking things that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future.”
“Monks, there is an undertaking of things that is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future.

In this regard, monks, one who is ignorant and immersed in ignorance does not understand, as it really is, that undertaking of things which is painful in the present and results in suffering in the future, thinking:
‘This indeed is an undertaking of things that is painful in the present and results in suffering in the future.’”
Not knowing that, being immersed in ignorance and not understanding it as it truly is, one pursues it and does not avoid it.
As one pursues it and does not avoid it, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable states increase, while desirable, pleasing, and agreeable states diminish. Why is that?
For it is thus, monks, that it happens for one who lacks wisdom.

In this regard, monks, regarding that undertaking of things which is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future, the ignorant person, being immersed in ignorance, does not understand it as it really is:
"This undertaking of things is indeed pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future."
Not knowing that, being immersed in ignorance and not understanding it as it truly is, one pursues it and does not avoid it.
For one who pursues it and does not avoid it, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable states increase, while desirable, pleasing, and agreeable states diminish.
What is the reason for this?
For it is thus, monks, with one who lacks knowledge.

In this regard, monks, regarding that undertaking of things which is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future, the ignorant person, being immersed in ignorance, does not understand it as it really is:
"This undertaking of things is indeed painful in the present but results in happiness in the future."
Not knowing that, being immersed in ignorance and not understanding it as it truly is, one does not cultivate it and avoids it.

As one does not cultivate it and avoids it, unwholesome states that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable increase, while wholesome states that are desirable, lovely, and agreeable decline. Why is that?
For it is thus, monks, that it happens for one who lacks knowledge.

In this regard, monks, when there is an undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future, the ignorant person, being immersed in ignorance, does not understand it as it truly is:
"This undertaking of a practice is indeed pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future."
Not knowing that, being immersed in ignorance and not understanding it as it truly is, one does not cultivate it and avoids it.
As one does not cultivate it and avoids it, unwholesome states that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable increase, while wholesome states that are desirable, lovely, and agreeable decline.
For what reason is that?
For it is thus, monks, that it happens for one who lacks wisdom.
In this regard, monks, a wise person possessing true knowledge understands, as it really is, that undertaking of things which is painful both in the present and results in suffering in the future:
"This indeed is an undertaking of things that is painful both in the present and results in suffering in the future."
One who knows this, being possessed of clear vision and understanding it as it truly is, does not pursue it but avoids it.

As he does not pursue it and avoids it, unwholesome states that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable diminish, while wholesome states that are desirable, lovely, and agreeable increase. Why is that?
For it is thus, monks, that it is for one who possesses wisdom.

In this regard, monks, regarding that undertaking of things which is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future, the wise person who has attained knowledge understands it as it really is:
"This indeed is an undertaking of things that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future."
Knowing this, one who has attained true knowledge and understands it as it really is does not pursue that [unwholesome state] but avoids it.
As he does not pursue it and avoids it, unwholesome states that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable diminish, while wholesome states that are desirable, lovely, and agreeable increase.
For what reason is that?
For it is thus, monks, that it is for one who has seen.

In this regard, monks, regarding that undertaking of things which is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future, the one who has seen and reached true knowledge understands it as it really is:
"This, indeed, is an undertaking of things that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future."
Knowing that, being possessed of clear vision, and understanding it as it truly is, one cultivates it and does not avoid it.
For one who cultivates it and does not avoid it, undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable states diminish, while desirable, pleasing, and agreeable states increase. Why is that?
For it is so, monks, with one who has seen.

Therein, monks, regarding that undertaking of things which is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future, the one who has seen and possesses knowledge understands it as it really is:
"This indeed is the undertaking of things which is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future."
Knowing that, one who has attained true knowledge and understands it as it really is cultivates that [state] and does not avoid it.
As he cultivates it and does not avoid it, undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable states diminish, while desirable, lovely, and agreeable states increase. Why is that?
For it is thus, monks, that it happens for one who possesses wisdom.
And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is painful both in the present and results in suffering in the future?
Here, monks, someone, with pain and with mental distress, takes life; and because of taking life, he experiences pain and mental distress.
Together with pain and together with mental distress, one takes what is not given, and because of taking what is not given, one experiences pain and mental distress;

together with pain and together with mental distress, one engages in sexual misconduct regarding sensual pleasures, and because of sexual misconduct regarding sensual pleasures, one experiences pain and mental distress;
together with pain and together with mental distress, one speaks falsehood, and because of speaking falsehood, one experiences pain and mental distress.
Together with pain and together with mental distress, one speaks maliciously; and because of that malicious speech, one experiences pain and mental distress.
Together with pain and together with mental distress, one speaks harshly; and because of that harsh speech, one experiences pain and mental distress.
Together with pain and together with mental distress, one indulges in idle chatter; and because of that idle chatter, one experiences pain and mental distress.
Together with suffering and together with mental distress, one is covetous; and conditioned by covetousness, one experiences suffering and mental distress.
Together with suffering and together with mental distress, one has a mind of ill will; and conditioned by ill will, one experiences suffering and mental distress.
Together with suffering and together with mental distress, one holds wrong view; and conditioned by wrong view, one experiences suffering and mental distress.
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is painful both in the present and results in pain in the future.
And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present but results in pain in the future?
“Here, monks, a certain person, together with pleasure and together with joy, takes life; and on account of taking life, he experiences pleasure and joy.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, he takes what is not given; and on account of taking what is not given, he experiences pleasure and joy.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, he engages in sexual misconduct; and on account of sexual misconduct, he experiences pleasure and joy.”
One speaks falsely together with pleasure and together with joy, and one experiences pleasure and joy as a result of speaking falsely;
one speaks divisively together with pleasure and together with joy, and one experiences pleasure and joy as a result of speaking divisively;
one speaks harshly together with pleasure and together with joy, and one experiences pleasure and joy as a result of speaking harshly.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, one engages in idle chatter, and through the condition of idle chatter, one experiences pleasure and joy;
together with pleasure and together with joy, one is covetous, and through the condition of covetousness, one experiences pleasure and joy;
together with pleasure and together with joy, one has a mind of ill will, and through the condition of ill will, one experiences pleasure and joy.
There is wrong view accompanied by pleasure and accompanied by joy, and one experiences pleasure and joy conditioned by that wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present but has a result of suffering in the future.
"And what, monks, is the undertaking of things that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future?
Here, monks, someone—with pain and with mental distress—abstains from the destruction of life, and because of that abstention from destroying life, he experiences pain and mental distress;
with pain and with mental distress, he abstains from taking what is not given, and because of that abstention from taking what is not given, he experiences pain and mental distress."
Together with pain and together with mental distress, he abstains from sexual misconduct, and on account of that abstinence from sexual misconduct, he experiences pain and mental distress;
together with pain and together with mental distress, he abstains from false speech, and on account of that abstinence from false speech, he experiences pain and mental distress;
together with pain and together with mental distress, he abstains from malicious speech, and on account of that abstinence from malicious speech, he experiences pain and mental distress.
Together with pain and together with mental distress, he abstains from harsh speech, and because of his abstinence from harsh speech, he experiences pain and mental distress;
together with pain and together with mental distress, he abstains from idle chatter, and because of his abstinence from idle chatter, he experiences pain and mental distress;
together with pain and together with mental distress, he is free from covetousness, and because of his freedom from covetousness, he experiences pain and mental distress.
Even with suffering and even with mental distress, his mind remains free from ill will; and on account of that non-ill will, he experiences suffering and mental distress.
Even with suffering and even with mental distress, he possesses right view; and on account of that right view, he experiences suffering and mental distress.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future.
And what, monks, is the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant both in the present and results in happiness in the future?
Here, monks, someone—with pleasure and with joy—abstains from taking life, and because of that abstention from taking life, he experiences pleasure and joy.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, he abstains from taking what is not given, and by reason of abstaining from taking what is not given, he experiences pleasure and joy;
together with pleasure and together with joy, he abstains from sexual misconduct, and by reason of abstaining from sexual misconduct, he experiences pleasure and joy;
together with pleasure and together with joy, he abstains from false speech, and by reason of abstaining from false speech, he experiences pleasure and joy.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, he abstains from malicious speech; and because of that abstinence from malicious speech, he experiences pleasure and joy.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, he abstains from harsh speech; and because of that abstinence from harsh speech, he experiences pleasure and joy.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, he abstains from idle chatter; and because of that abstinence from idle chatter, he experiences pleasure and joy.
Together with pleasure and together with joy, one is free from covetousness, and by reason of that freedom from covetousness, one experiences pleasure and joy;
together with pleasure and together with joy, one has a mind free from ill will, and by reason of that freedom from ill will, one experiences pleasure and joy;
together with pleasure and together with joy, one possesses right view, and by reason of that right view, one experiences pleasure and joy.
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
This, monks, is called the undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future.
These, monks, are the four undertakings of practice.
“Monks, it is just as if there were a bitter gourd mixed with poison.
Then a man might come along, desiring life, not wishing for death, seeking happiness, and averse to suffering.
They would say to him:”
“O man, this bitter gourd is mixed with poison;
if you wish, drink it.
As you drink it, it will not please you in its color, smell, or taste; and having drunk it, you will meet death or suffer pain equal to death.”
Thus, without reflecting, he might drink it and not relinquish it.
While drinking it, it would not please him in its color, smell, or taste; and having drunk it, he would meet death or suffer pain amounting to death.
Monks, I say that this undertaking of dhamma is just like that—an undertaking of dhamma that is painful in the present and results in pain in the future.
“Monks, it is just as if there were a bronze vessel of beverage, perfect in color, perfect in fragrance,
and perfect in taste, but mixed with poison.
Then a man might come along, desiring life, not desiring death, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering.”
They would say to him:
"O man, this bronze vessel of drink is endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of flavor;
however, it is mixed with poison."
“If you desire it, drink.
While you are drinking it, it will indeed please you in its color, fragrance, and flavor; but having drunk it, you will meet death or experience suffering equal to death.
If he were to drink it without reflecting and not relinquish it, [he would suffer].
While he was drinking it, it might indeed please him in its color, its fragrance, and its flavor; yet after drinking it, he would meet death or experience suffering amounting to death.
Monks, I say that this undertaking of a practice is just like that: an undertaking of a practice that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future.
It is, monks, just as if there were putrid urine mixed with various medicinal herbs.
Then a man might come who was afflicted with jaundice.
They would say to him:
"O man, this putrid urine is mixed with various medicines; if you wish, drink it."
‘While you are drinking it, it will not please you in its color, smell, or taste; yet after you have drunk it, you will become happy.
Having reflected thus, he would drink it and would not relinquish it.
While he was drinking it, it would indeed not please him in its color, smell, or taste; yet after having drunk it, he would be happy.
“Monks, I say that this undertaking of the Dhamma is just like that: it is an undertaking of the Dhamma that is painful in the present but results in happiness in the future.
It is just as if, monks, there were curd, honey, ghee, and molasses all mixed together in one place.
Then a man would come along suffering from a hemorrhage.”
They would say to him:
"O man, here is curd, honey, ghee, and molasses mixed together in one place; if you wish, drink it.
As you drink it, it will satisfy you with its color, fragrance, and flavor, and having drunk it, you will become happy."
Having reflected thus, he would drink it and would not reject it.
As he drank it, it would satisfy him in its color, fragrance, and flavor, and having drunk it, he would be happy.
Monks, I say that this undertaking of the Dhamma is similar: it is an undertaking of the Dhamma that is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future.
Just as, monks, in the last month of the rains, at the time of autumn, when the sky is clear and free from clouds,
the sun, rising into the heavens, dispelling all the darkness spread across the atmosphere, shines, glows, and radiates;

“In the very same way, monks, this undertaking of the Dhamma, which is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future, outshines, outblazes, and outshines all other doctrines of ordinary recluses and brahmins.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Sixth Discourse on the Undertaking of Great Dhamma is finished.
